Unit 7: Machine Intelligence

SL curriculum overview and structured learning plan.

Introduction

How can machines learn from experience without explicit programming?

This unit introduces the shift from Deterministic Programming (where we write the rules) to Machine Learning (where the computer finds the rules). You'll explore the taxonomy of AI, the specialized hardware that powers it, and the ethical dilemmas of algorithmic decision-making.

You'll begin by defining Narrow AI vs General AI. Then, you'll categorize different types of learning (Supervised, Unsupervised, Reinforcement), examine the GPUs and TPUs that drive them, and finally debate the ethics of Bias and Accountability.

Taxonomy of Learning

Machine Learning isn't one thing. It's a family of techniques:

  • Supervised Learning: Training with labeled data (e.g., "This image is a cat").
  • Unsupervised Learning: Finding patterns in unlabeled data (e.g., "These customers buy similar things").
  • Reinforcement Learning: Learning through trial and error (reward/punishment).
  • Deep Learning: Using multi-layered Neural Networks.
  • Transfer Learning: Reusing a pre-trained model for a new task.
AI Hardware

AI requires massive parallel processing power. Traditional CPUs are too sequential.

  • GPU (Graphics Processing Unit): Originally for games, now used for parallel AI math.
  • TPU (Tensor Processing Unit): Custom hardware designed by Google specifically for neural networks.
  • ASIC / Edge: Specialized chips running AI directly on devices (like phones) without the cloud.
Ethics of AI

With great power comes great responsibility. We must solve the "Black Box" problem:

  • Bias: If training data is prejudiced, the AI will be prejudiced.
  • Accountability: Who is responsible if an autonomous car crashes?
  • Transparency: Can we explain why the AI made a decision?
Key Terminology
TermDefinition
Artificial Intelligence (AI) Systems that perform tasks that normally require human intelligence (visual perception, speech recognition, decision-making).
Narrow AI AI designed for a specific task (e.g., Chess, Spam filters). This is the only AI we have today.
General AI (AGI) Hypothetical AI that can understand any intellectual task that a human can. (Does not exist yet).
Machine Learning A subset of AI where computers learn from data without being explicitly programmed for specific rules.
Supervised Learning Learning where the model is trained on a labeled dataset (Input-Output pairs).
Unsupervised Learning Learning where the model looks for undetected patterns in a data set with no pre-existing labels.
Reinforcement Learning Learning by interacting with an environment; receiving positive rewards or negative penalties.
Deep Learning Machine learning based on artificial neural networks with multiple layers (hence 'deep').
GPU / TPU Processors optimized for the parallel calculations required by neural networks.
Algorithmic Bias Systematic and repeatable errors in a computer system that create unfair outcomes, often due to biased training data.
